declarations.description:
CodeMirror, not a `<textarea>`. The textarea it replaces was the right call
while a sandbox only had to hold text: undo, selection, spellcheck
suppression, mobile keyboards, and screen-reader support all came from the
platform. What it could not do is highlight what it holds, number its lines,
or say where the cursor is, and a status bar reading line and column has to
ask something.

**On its own path.** This is `@helix-io/sandbox/editor` rather than part of
the barrel, because CodeMirror is around 110 KB over the wire where the rest
of this package is a few. A sandbox with no editable pane should not pay for
one, and neither should a site that registers its elements once.

The view is built once and reconfigured, not rebuilt. Replacing it on every
change would throw away the undo history, the scroll position, and the
selection, which is most of what an editor is.
declarations.name: HelixSandboxEditor

`root` is the shadow root rather than the document, or CodeMirror puts its
stylesheet where this element cannot see it and the editor renders unstyled.

members.name: focus
members.description:
Moves focus into the text, not onto the host.

The host is not focusable: what a reader types into is CodeMirror's
contenteditable, several nodes down inside this shadow root. Without this,
`editor.focus()` from outside silently does nothing.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

declarations.name: highlightStyle
declarations.description:
How source is coloured, in Helix tokens.

CodeMirror ships `defaultHighlightStyle`, which is a fixed set of hex values
and therefore one palette in both colour modes: readable on white, wrong on
anything else. These are `--helix-color-syntax-*`, which resolve through
`light-dark()` like every other colour in the system, so the editor follows
the page rather than declaring its own mode.

The palette is GitHub's, which is what the sandbox this replaces used, and
what most engineers already read without having to learn it.

A tag not named here inherits the editor's foreground. That is deliberate:
punctuation, operators and separators are structure a reader skims past, and
colouring them competes with the names that carry the meaning.

A same-origin `<iframe>` pointed at `src`, which is a document the consumer
provides. That document imports whatever the examples need, listens for a
render message, and writes the markup into itself.

**A frame rather than the page.** Rendering into the page meant an example
was styled by whatever surrounded it, which flatters the preview and lies
about it: an example that restyles `helix-card` restyled the sandbox too, a
script in an example ran against the real document, and a stray
`position: fixed` escaped the pane. It also left nothing to capture console
output from, and the terminal has to come from somewhere.

The cost is that the frame starts empty. Styles and element definitions do
not cross into it, because a document has its own stylesheets and a window
has its own custom element registry, so `src` has to load them. That is the
consumer's document rather than something guessed at here.

**The source is trusted.** It is markup a developer typed into their own
sandbox. Never point this at input from anyone else.
declarations.name: HelixSandboxPreview

declarations.summary: Renders sandbox source in a frame of its own.

declarations.description:
Coordination is by event, the same way the accordion does it: a source pane
dispatches `SourceChange`, which bubbles, and the sandbox hands the value to
whatever preview is slotted into it. Neither child knows the other exists, so
either can be replaced or used alone.

The event carries the pane's `name`, which is what lets one sandbox hold a
markup pane and a stylesheet pane without the root identifying senders by
reference. `css` becomes the preview's stylesheet; anything else is markup.

The split is a real `role="separator"` with `aria-valuenow`, movable by
pointer and by arrow keys, because a divider that only responds to dragging
is unusable without a mouse. Home and End jump to the bounds.
declarations.name: HelixSandbox

members.name: fromSource
members.description:
Whether a change came from inside this sandbox's source region.

Structural rather than a type check. It was `instanceof
HelixSandboxSource`, which was right until there was a second kind of
pane: the editor is `@helix-io/sandbox/editor`, on its own path because it
carries CodeMirror, and naming its class here would pull that back into
this module for every consumer. Where the event came from is a question
about the tree, and the tree can answer it.

members.name: handleSourceChange
members.description:
Takes a change from one of this sandbox's own source panes.

The origin is checked, and has to be. `helix-change` bubbles and composes,
so anything a consumer slots into a sandbox sends one up here too. A
sandbox hears a great deal that is not its source.

members.name: handleCaret
members.description:
Writes the cursor position onto any status bar slotted here.

The same shape as the source-to-preview hand-off, and for the same reason:
the editor and the bar never speak, so either can be absent. It goes
straight to the element rather than through a property a framework owns,
because this fires on every keystroke and every arrow press.

members.name: parts
members.description:
The parts of this sandbox it drives, wherever they sit inside it.

Descendants, not children. A preview and a status bar happen to be slotted
directly, but a terminal lives inside the tab set that holds the panel, so
a search of `children` found none and the console went nowhere. Where a
consumer nests a pane is their arrangement to make.

Client only: the server has no children to read.

members.name: handleConsole
members.description:
Hands a console line from the preview to any terminal slotted here.

Every `helix-console` is forwarded, with no check on where it came from.
Unlike a change, which any form control in a sandbox emits, this event is
dispatched by exactly one thing: a preview relaying what the document
inside its frame wrote. There is nothing else here it could be confused
with.

members.name: axis
members.description:
The orientation in force.

Unset is horizontal, and stays unset: the default is the absent attribute,
so a reflected default cannot appear on the host after hydration.

members.name: applySplit
members.description:
Writes the split into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, because an inline style on
the host is an attribute the element gives itself once it upgrades, and a
React consumer's server markup does not have it: hydration reports the
mismatch and does not patch it up. The shadow root is not part of the tree
React hydrates.

Filled imperatively because Lit rejects expressions inside `<style>`, which
is why the template carries a static empty one. The server renders the
stylesheet's default split, which is the same 45% this property defaults
to.

declarations.description:
A real `<textarea>`, not a contenteditable div with a syntax highlighter over
it. Undo, selection, spellcheck suppression, mobile keyboards, and screen
reader support all come from the platform, and every one of them is
expensive to rebuild and easy to get subtly wrong.

that cannot indent is not one. Escape then Tab still moves focus out, which
is the documented escape hatch for exactly this trade.

declarations.description:
Slotted into a sandbox, which feeds it: the editor dispatches `helix-caret`
on every keystroke and every arrow press, the sandbox hears it and writes the
position here. Nothing about that reaches the consumer's framework, which is
the point. A caret position routed through React state would re-render the
workbench on every cursor move, to update two numbers.

**Not a live region.** The readout changes on every keystroke, so announcing
it would talk over the reader continuously while they type. It is text they
can navigate to, which is what a status bar is in every editor that has one.

A readout with nothing to say is not rendered at all rather than rendered
empty, or the bar keeps a gap where a value is not.
declarations.name: HelixSandboxStatusBar

declarations.description:
Fed by the sandbox, which hears `helix-console` from the preview and hands it
here. The preview is a separate document, so what arrives has already crossed
`postMessage`: text, not values.

**Repeats collapse.** An example with a render loop can write the same
warning hundreds of times, and two hundred identical lines say nothing that
one line and a count does not. Only consecutive repeats collapse, so the
order of what happened survives.

A `role="log"` rather than a live region by hand. It is the semantic for an
append-only stream, and it means a reader is told about new output without
the whole panel being re-announced each time.
declarations.name: HelixSandboxTerminal

members.name: following
members.description:
Whether the reader is at the bottom, and so wants to follow new output.

Read before the render that adds a line and applied after it. Scrolling to
the bottom on every line would drag a reader off whatever they had scrolled
up to look at, which for a log of errors is the one thing they are doing.

members.name: write
members.description:
Adds a line, collapsing it into the one above when they are identical.

`write` rather than `append`, which every element already has from
`ParentNode` and which takes nodes. Shadowing it would break
`terminal.append(node)` for anyone who reasonably expected the DOM method.
